# Module 05 — Finite Fields

> **Goal.** Everything about F_q for q = p^n: existence, uniqueness,
> subfields, and above all the **Frobenius automorphism**. Special focus
> on F_{p²}, home of the supersingular world.
>
> **Lab:** [`lab02_finite_fields.py`](../labs/lab02_finite_fields.py)

## 1. Classification

**Theorem.** (i) Every finite field has order q = p^n, p prime (its
characteristic). (ii) For every such q there is a field of order q,
unique up to isomorphism: **F_q**. (iii) F_{p^m} ⊆ F_{p^n} iff m | n.

*Why order p^n:* a finite field K contains F_p (generated by 1) and is a
finite-dimensional F_p-vector space, so |K| = p^dim.

*Why unique/existent:* every element satisfies x^q = x (Lagrange in K^×
plus 0), so K is exactly the set of roots of x^q − x in an algebraic
closure; one checks that root set *is* a field (closed under +, × by
Frobenius, §3) and that x^q − x is squarefree. One polynomial, one root
set, one field.

The identity worth framing:

  **x^q − x = ∏_{c ∈ F_q} (x − c)**

Lab 06 exploits it directly: gcd(f(x), x^q − x) extracts from f exactly
its roots lying in F_q — that is how we find 2-torsion x-coordinates
over F_{p²} without ever leaving polynomial arithmetic.

In practice (module 03 §5): F_{p^n} = F_p[x]/(f) for any irreducible f
of degree n. Different f, same field, different coordinates.

## 2. F_{p²} concretely

Take a quadratic non-residue ns ∈ F_p (module 04) and set

  F_{p²} = F_p(u), u² = ns = {a + bu : a, b ∈ F_p}.

* Multiplication: (a + bu)(c + du) = (ac + bd·ns) + (ad + bc)u.
* Inversion via the **norm**: define N(a + bu) = (a + bu)(a − bu) =
  a² − ns·b² ∈ F_p; then (a + bu)⁻¹ = (a − bu)/N(a + bu). (Rationalize
  the denominator — same trick as for ℂ.)
* For p ≡ 3 (mod 4) we can take ns = −1 and write i for u: complex
  arithmetic mod p. Lab 02's `Fp2` prints elements as `a+b*i` in this
  case.

**Squares migrate.** Every element of F_p^× is a square in F_{p²}:
for c ∈ F_p^×, c^((p²−1)/2) = (c^((p−1)/2))^(p+1) = (±1)^(even) = 1.
So a non-square of F_{p²} is genuinely quadratic — lab 02's `sqrt` must
hunt for one at random before running Tonelli–Shanks. Euler's criterion,
Tonelli–Shanks, Lagrange: all of module 04 runs verbatim with p − 1
replaced by p² − 1.

## 3. Frobenius

**π : x ↦ x^p** is an automorphism of F_{p^n} (freshman's dream for the
homomorphism property, finiteness for bijectivity), fixing exactly F_p
(the roots of x^p − x). The automorphism group of F_{p^n}/F_p is cyclic
of order n, generated by π — Galois theory of finite fields in one line.

On F_{p²}: π has order 2, and with the u² = ns presentation,

  π(a + bu) = a − bu — **conjugation**,

because u^p = u·(u²)^((p−1)/2) = u·ns^((p−1)/2) = −u (ns is a
non-residue: Euler's criterion). Fixed points = F_p; π² = id;
N(x) = x·π(x) = x^(p+1). All verified programmatically in lab 02's
self-checks.

Why care so much? Three escalating reasons:

1. **membership test**: x ∈ F_p ⟺ x^p = x — how lab 06 could check
   whether a j-invariant lies in the subfield F_p (the Delfs–Galbraith
   attack surface, module 10);
2. **point counting**: Frobenius acts on the points of a curve defined
   over F_p, and its "trace" counts points — the Hasse bound and
   Schoof's algorithm are theorems about π (module 07);
3. **Frobenius is itself an isogeny** — the prototypical *inseparable*
   one (module 09), and whether π commutes with a curve's other
   endomorphisms is *the* dividing line between ordinary and
   supersingular curves (module 08).

## 4. The algebraic closure

F̄_p = ⋃_n F_{p^n}: every polynomial over any F_{p^n} splits somewhere
up the tower. Geometry "over F̄_p" (all torsion points, all isogenies,
all j-invariants) is where clean theorems live; computations then pick
the smallest field containing what they touch. The recurring miracle of
this course: for supersingular curves, that field is **always F_{p²}**
(module 08) — the infinite tower collapses to one story.

## 5. Norm and trace (used quietly later)

For x ∈ F_{p²}: Tr(x) = x + x^p ∈ F_p and N(x) = x·x^p = x^(p+1) ∈ F_p.
The norm is multiplicative and surjective onto F_p^×; the trace is
F_p-linear and surjective. (Lab 02, exercise 2.2 has you verify the norm
claim empirically.)

## 6. Self-check

<details><summary><b>Q1.</b> Why is there no field with 6 elements?</summary>

6 = 2·3 is not a prime power. A field of characteristic 2 has 2^n
elements (F_p-vector space); characteristic 3 gives 3^n; 6 is neither.
</details>

<details><summary><b>Q2.</b> In F_9 = F_3(u), u² = −1 (check −1 is a
non-square mod 3), compute (1 + u)⁴.</summary>

(1+u)² = 1 + 2u + u² = 2u (since u² = −1 = 2 and 1 + 2 = 0 in F_3).
Then (2u)² = 4u² = 1·(−1) = −1 = 2. So (1+u)⁴ = 2, and (1+u)⁸ = 4 = 1:
the element 1 + u has order 8 = 9 − 1, a generator of F_9^× — finite
field multiplicative groups are cyclic in action.
</details>

<details><summary><b>Q3.</b> How many elements of F_{p²} satisfy
x^p = x? Satisfy x^p = −x?</summary>

x^p = x: exactly the subfield F_p, p elements. x^p = −x: the "trace
zero" set; with u² = ns presentation it is {bu}, again p elements
(includes 0). For p ≡ 3 (mod 4): purely imaginary elements.
</details>

<details><summary><b>Q4.</b> The polynomial x⁴ + 1 factors modulo
<i>every</i> prime, though it is irreducible over ℚ. Explain via F_{p²}.</summary>

Its roots are primitive 8th roots of unity; 8 | p² − 1 for every odd p
(p² ≡ 1 mod 8, module 04), so the roots already live in F_{p²}: each
root generates at most a degree-2 extension, forcing quadratic (or
linear) factors. Moral: subfield structure controls factorization —
the same logic that pins supersingular j-invariants into F_{p²}.
</details>

## 7. Where this goes

Fields: done. Now geometry. Module 06 defines elliptic curves over
these fields and builds their group law; from there every object of
modules 07–11 (Frobenius traces, torsion, isogenies, graphs) is
algebra over F_p and F_{p²} — precisely the two classes you now have
implemented, tested, in `lab02_finite_fields.py`.
